title: Experiment assignment options brainstorm (route-level A/B testing)
content:
Context
- We’re adding route-level experiments at the routing layer. Core constraint: assignment must be deterministic (same user -> same variant) across retries, across regions (as much as possible), and across time (as long as config is stable).
- We need a “stickiness key” used as input to deterministic bucketing. Customers may or may not provide an explicit key.
- Goal of this doc: brainstorm assignment mechanisms + evaluate entropy/collision risk + operational implications (debuggability, privacy, compatibility with existing routing/policy engine).

Non-goals (for this brainstorm)
- Statistical analysis / significance engine.
- Multi-region population rebalancing (we only need consistent deterministic bucketing given a key).

Terminology
- stickiness key: the stable identifier we hash to assign a request to a bucket/variant.
- assignment inputs: (experiment_id, stickiness_key, maybe route_id) -> hash -> bucket -> variant.
- entropy: how many unique values we reasonably expect for the key in typical workloads (important for split accuracy).
- collision: different real users producing identical stickiness_key (or effectively identical due to low cardinality) leading to skew.

Key requirements (must-haves)
1) Deterministic across retries and streaming restarts.
2) Safe defaults when key missing (must not silently produce pathological skew).
3) Doesn’t leak PII / aligns with security posture (audit + logs).
4) Works across hosted/dedicated/private deployments.
5) Debuggable: support and on-call can explain “why did I get variant B?”
6) Doesn’t explode metrics cardinality.

Candidate assignment mechanisms
We’re considering (not mutually exclusive):
A) Explicit customer-provided header (e.g., X-Redwood-Sticky-Key)
B) Customer/account identifier (customer_id / org_id)
C) Session-based identifiers (session_id) provided by customer or derived from our own gateway
D) End-user identifier (user_id) passed by customer
E) Request-derived fallback (IP, user-agent, request_id)

High-level take: The best primary mechanism is explicit customer-provided stickiness (A), with documented precedence and strong validation/warnings. Then a safe fallback chain that is predictable and minimizes skew.

Option comparison table (rough)

1) Header-based: X-Redwood-Sticky-Key (customer sets)
- Determinism: High (if stable)
- Entropy: Depends on customer; can be very high (user ids) or very low (constant string)
- Collision risk: Depends on customer; can be catastrophic if they set it incorrectly
- Pros:
  - Works for all customers and routing contexts (chat/completions/embeddings)
  - Allows true end-user stickiness vs account-level stickiness
  - Cross-region consistency is good if same header is used
  - Easy to support “same user pinned to same variant”
- Cons:
  - Customers need to implement; easiest to forget
  - Risk of accidental low entropy -> split skew (e.g., using “true/false” or a fixed value)
  - Potential PII concerns if they pass raw emails, etc.
- Operational implications:
  - We must provide validation + warnings in Console + docs
  - We must redact/avoid logging raw header; only log derived hash or truncated diagnostic
  - Debug endpoint needs to show whether this was used + basic quality checks (length/entropy heuristics)
- Notes:
  - Provide SDK helpers to set this header and strongly recommend “stable opaque id”, not email.

2) customer_id / org_id-based (derived from auth)
- Determinism: High
- Entropy: Usually moderate-to-low in context of a single route (one org -> single key)
- Collision risk: Low for uniqueness, but functionally causes “all users in org get same variant”
- Pros:
  - No customer implementation needed
  - Safe from a PII perspective (internal ID)
  - Very stable and consistent across regions
  - Great for experiments intended to compare org-level behavior (rare)
- Cons:
  - Not a real A/B test for end users; it’s an “account split” (entire customer is one bucket)
  - Breaks split accuracy goals within a single customer; Console results can be misleading for high-volume single-tenant customers
  - Creates awkward scenario: a single enterprise customer might be entirely on variant B and think it’s “random”
- Operational implications:
  - Works as fallback only; should be clearly labeled as account-level stickiness
  - Might be acceptable for internal experiments / dogfooding where traffic spans many orgs

3) Session-based (customer-provided session_id)
- Determinism: Medium-to-high (session lifetime matters)
- Entropy: High if many sessions
- Collision risk: Low if session IDs are well-formed; but depends on customer
- Pros:
  - Common for web apps; often easier than true user_id
  - Gives reasonable distribution even if user ids are sparse
- Cons:
  - Sessions rotate; users can “flip variants” between sessions
  - If sessions are short-lived, experiment results can be noisy (variant mixing)
- Operational implications:
  - We can support as a documented “good enough” option
  - Needs guidance: choose session_id if user_id not available, but expect cross-session variance

4) End-user identifier (customer-provided user_id)
- Determinism: High
- Entropy: High
- Collision risk: Low if properly unique
- Pros:
  - Best for true user-level A/B
  - Good cross-region consistency if stable
- Cons:
  - PII risk if they pass raw identifiers (email/phone)
  - Some customers don’t have user ids (B2B APIs)
- Operational implications:
  - We should not prescribe user_id specifically; we prescribe “opaque stable ID”
  - Must treat incoming values as potentially sensitive; never log raw

5) Request-derived fallback (IP, user-agent, request_id)
- Determinism: Low-to-medium
- Entropy: Variable; often problematic
- Collision risk: High in NAT/proxy environments; request_id is high entropy but NOT stable
- Pros:
  - “Always available” (especially request_id)
- Cons:
  - request_id: guarantees near-perfect split distribution but destroys stickiness (every request random)
  - IP: poor uniqueness for large networks; also privacy/regulatory issues; can change frequently
  - user-agent: extremely low entropy
- Operational implications:
  - Should not be default fallback except as an explicit “random assignment per request” mode
  - If we must fallback, request_id should only be used if experiment is flagged as non-sticky / sampling-based (probably out of scope)

Entropy/collision deep dive (why we care)
- If stickiness_key has low entropy within the population for a given route, traffic splits will skew hard.
  - Example: key = customer_id for a route dominated by a single customer => 100% of that customer hits one variant.
  - Example: key = “true” because customer mistakenly passes boolean => 100% of traffic -> one bucket.
- Even with a decent key, you can get skew if:
  - key is missing for a subset of traffic and fallback path differs
  - key differs across regions due to different upstream services
  - key includes unstable components (timestamp, request_id)
- Simple heuristics we can apply (server-side) to warn customers:
  - key length too short (< 8 chars) => warn (not block)
  - key equals one of a small set of common constants ("0", "1", "true", "false", "unknown", "null") => warn (and consider blocking for GA?)
  - observed unique-key cardinality in last N minutes is extremely low compared to request volume => alert / banner (“low entropy key”) (needs telemetry support)

Operational considerations

Precedence order proposal (for ADR; tentative)
1) X-Redwood-Sticky-Key (explicit)
2) X-Redwood-Session-Id (optional secondary explicit) OR a single header with semantics “opaque id” (we should avoid many headers)
3) customer_id (internal) ONLY IF experiment is configured to allow account-level stickiness
4) If none available:
   - default = “assignment disabled” (treat experiment as not applicable) OR
   - default = route-level safe fallback that does not produce silent skew

Important: we should not silently fall back to customer_id if the customer intended user-level splits; that turns into a surprising account-level pin.

Two modes worth considering
- Strict mode (recommended for GA): experiment requires a stickiness key (explicit header). If missing, request is excluded from experiment (variant = control) and attribution marks “ineligible_missing_key”.
- Lenient mode (beta/internal): allow fallback to customer_id and/or “random per request” based on explicit config.

Eligibility + attribution
- We should tag attribution with:
  - assignment_source = header | customer_id | none
  - eligibility_reason = eligible | missing_key | invalid_key | experiment_paused | config_stale
- This is critical for debugging and for Console to explain data gaps.

Debuggability requirements
- Internal debug endpoint should display:
  - which key source was used (but not raw key)
  - hash input components used (experiment_id, key source, normalized key length, optional route_id)
  - selected variant + bucket boundaries
  - config version + time loaded (helps with propagation lag)
- Support playbook needs a simple answer to: “why did my split skew?” => typically missing or low-entropy key.

Privacy/security
- Never store raw stickiness keys in logs, traces, or metrics.
- If we need correlation, store a salted hash (salt = per-environment secret) so the same key is stable for debugging but cannot be reversed.
- Console should display only:
  - “key present: yes/no”
  - “key source: explicit header/customer_id”
  - “entropy warning: low/ok (based on aggregate)”
- If enterprise customers want to use email, docs should explicitly discourage it; suggest hashing client-side.

Cross-region consistency
- If customer sends the same header to all regions, hashing is consistent.
- If we fall back to customer_id, it is consistent across regions.
- If we fall back to IP/user-agent, consistency is poor and privacy risk increases.

Metrics/observability
- Major risk: adding experiment_id + variant_id as dimensions increases cardinality.
  - Proposed mitigation: only tag experiment metrics for requests where experiment is active + eligible.
  - Consider sampling debug-level traces with expanded tags.
- We should track:
  - attribution_drop_rate = % of requests expected to be in experiment but missing experiment tags
  - key_missing_rate per route/experiment
  - assignment_source distribution (header vs fallback)

Known failure modes (early list)
- Missing sticky key on streaming retries => attribution disappears on retry path
- Customer sends sticky key only on some endpoints (chat vs completions) causing partial eligibility
- Config propagation lag causes different assignment behavior between regions during rollout
- Customer uses low-entropy key -> skew; Console shows “broken experiment”

Open questions
1) Do we want one header (X-Redwood-Sticky-Key) with guidance “set this to user_id/session_id/whatever stable”, vs multiple headers (user-id, session-id)?
   - Leaning one header to keep it simple; add SDK convenience wrappers.
2) Should missing key exclude from experiment (control) or randomize? Excluding can bias results if missingness isn’t random.
   - For GA, excluding seems safer operationally. Provide explicit “random assignment” option later.
3) Should we include route_id in the hash input?
   - Pros: avoids correlation across experiments/contexts if same key used.
   - Cons: if a user hits multiple routes, variant assignment differs per route (could be fine). This is route-level experiment anyway.
4) Minimum key validation rules: warn vs hard reject?

Action items
- Jordan/Jada: propose precedence + strict/lenient mode in ADR-047 update (or follow-up ADR).
- Logan/Allison: define telemetry fields: assignment_source, eligibility_reason; update attribution schema draft.
- Kaitlyn/Marcus: confirm privacy posture on salted-hash logging for debug endpoint.
- DevEx: add docs language + SDK helper proposal for “sticky key best practices”.

Appendix: minimal recommendation (what we should tell customers)
- Provide X-Redwood-Sticky-Key on every request for routes in experiments.
- Use a stable opaque identifier per end user (or per session if no user id).
- Do not use email/phone; hash client-side if necessary.
- Ensure the key is present on streaming retries and tool-calling subrequests.

(End of doc — still draft; add examples once header naming is finalized.)
